title: Capital Gains Tax Exemption: How Section 54EC Bonds Can Help
description: Selling land or property can lead to significant long-term capital gains tax liabilities. Section 54EC of the Income Tax Act offers an exemption if you reinve.

faq.q: What is the primary purpose of Section 54EC?
faq.a: Section 54EC aims to encourage taxpayers to reinvest their long-term capital gains from the sale of land or building into specific infrastructure bonds, thereby providing them with a tax exemption on those gains.

faq.q: Can I invest more than ₹50 lakhs in 54EC bonds?
faq.a: While you can invest more than ₹50 lakhs, the maximum amount of long-term capital gains that can be exempted under Section 54EC in a financial year is capped at ₹50 lakhs. Any amount invested beyond this limit will not qualify for the exemption.

faq.q: What if I sell two properties in different financial years?
faq.a: The ₹50 lakh investment limit applies per financial year. If you sell one property in FY 2023-24 and another in FY 2024-25, you can claim an exemption of up to ₹50 lakhs for each financial year, provided you meet all other conditions for each sale.

faq.q: Are the interest earnings from 54EC bonds taxable?
faq.a: Yes, the interest earned on Section 54EC bonds is fully taxable as "Income from Other Sources" in the hands of the investor. The tax exemption only applies to the capital gains reinvested, not the interest income.

faq.q: What happens if I take a loan against these bonds?
faq.a: If you take a loan or advance against the Section 54EC bonds before the completion of their five-year lock-in period, the capital gains initially exempted will become taxable in the financial year in which the loan is taken.

Yes, Non-Resident Indians (NRIs) are generally eligible to invest in Section 54EC bonds, provided they meet all other conditions specified in the Income Tax Act. They would typically need to invest through an NRO account.

fact_check.summary: The article provides largely accurate information regarding Section 54EC bonds, their eligibility, conditions, investment limits, and lock-in periods, aligning well with current Indian tax laws. However, there's a minor discrepancy regarding the tax rate on long-term capital gains for assets like real estate, which has been updated in recent budgets.
